summary: Surveys the state of IPv6 deployment as of 2022. It looks at how widely it is used, discusses remaining challenges, and suggests areas that need further investigation. It obsoletes RFC 6036.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 is the newer version of the addressing system that the Internet runs on, and the move to it has been slow and uneven. This RFC takes stock: how many IPv4 addresses are left, how many people can reach the Internet over IPv6, and how many websites answer over IPv6. It then describes the ways networks have moved, from running both versions side by side to dropping IPv4 altogether, and sets out what still makes the move hard.

questions: what are the challenges of ipv6 adoption
what is ipv4 as a service
subtitle: A survey of how far the move from IPv4 to IPv6 has got, and what is still in the way.

tldr.problem: The last survey of IPv6 deployment was written in 2010, before mobile networks ran out of IPv4 addresses, before governments started requiring IPv6, and before the module of large providers became IPv6-only.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gathers the published measurements on IPv4 scarcity, IPv6 users and IPv6-reachable web content, surveys how service providers, enterprises and universities have deployed IPv6, and describes the five deployment scenarios and the challenges that remain.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 6036. It finds that IPv6-capable users passed 29 percent of all Internet users in January 2022, and that the remaining obstacles are operational rather than technical.

facts.label: Available IPv4 pool at the end of 2021
facts.value: 5.2 million addresses, with another 12.1 million reserved

facts.label: IPv6-capable users in January 2022
facts.value: 1,207.61 million, or 29.5 percent of Internet users

facts.label: IPv6-capable websites in January 2022
facts.value: 20.6 percent, up from 11.4 percent in January 2018

today: RFC 9386 was published in April 2023 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 6036, the previous deployment survey. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The document is a snapshot of the position in early 2022, with its measurements dated to 1 January 2022.

sections.title: Why Another Status Survey
sections.content:
RFC 6036 described IPv6 deployment scenarios that were adopted or foreseen by the service providers who responded to a technical questionnaire in early 2010, and it set out practices and plans expected to take place in the following years. Since then several other documents have contributed to the discussion: RFC 6180 discusses deployment models and transition mechanisms and recommends those proven effective in operational networks, RFC 6883 gives guidance for content and application service providers, and RFC 7381 introduces deployment guidelines for enterprises. RFC 6540 recommends IPv6 support to all IP-capable nodes, and it was referenced in the IAB statement on IPv6, which represented a major step in driving the IETF and other standards bodies towards using IPv6 in their work.

Considering all of that, and more than ten years since RFC 6036 was published, the RFC says it is useful to assess the status of the transition to IPv6. It gives three reasons. In some areas the lack of IPv4 addresses forced both carriers and content providers to shift to IPv6 to support new applications, in particular in wireless networks. Some governmental actions took place to encourage or even enforce IPv6 adoption in certain countries. And looking at global adoption, this seems to have reached a threshold that justifies speaking of end-to-end IPv6 connectivity, at least at the IPv6 service layer.

The document aims to survey the status of IPv6 deployment and highlight both the achievements and the remaining obstacles in the transition to IPv6 networks and their coexistence with continued IPv4 services. It is written for a general audience interested in the status of IPv6 in different industries and network domains, and attention is given to the different stages of the transition, with particular attention to the terminology around IPv6-only, which it treats as the final stage.
sections.plainLanguage: Ten years and one address shortage later, the picture had changed enough to be worth measuring again. The survey exists because operators and policy makers were working from a decade-old picture, and because the remaining questions are now about operations, training and money rather than about whether the protocol works.

sections.title: What IPv6-only Means at Each Level
sections.content:
The RFC defines the term IPv6-only in relation to the specific scope it refers to, and it may be that only part of a service, a network or even a node is in an IPv6-only scope while the rest is not. An IPv6-only interface is an interface configured to forward only IPv6, which denotes that just part of the node can be IPv6-only, since the rest of the interfaces of the same node may work with IPv4 as well; a Dual-Stack interface is not an IPv6-only interface. An IPv6-only node uses only IPv6, with all interfaces of the host having only IPv6 addresses.

An IPv6-only service is used if, between the host's interface and the interface of the content server, all packet headers of the service session are IPv6. An IPv6-only overlay is used if, between the endpoints of the tunnels, all inner packet headers of the tunnels are IPv6; in a fixed network, an IPv6-only overlay means the encapsulation is only IPv6 between the interfaces of the Provider Edge nodes, or between the Customer Provider Edge node and the Broadband Network Gateway. An IPv6-only underlay is used if the data plane and control plane are IPv6, though this is not necessarily true for the management plane; Segment Routing over IPv6 is an example of an IPv6-only underlay.

An IPv6-only network is used if every node in it is IPv6-only, and IPv4 should not exist in it. In particular, its data plane, control plane and management plane must all be IPv6, and all Provider Edge nodes must be IPv6-only, so if tunnels exist among them, both the inner and the outer headers must be IPv6.

IPv4-as-a-Service is the case where IPv4 service support is provided by means of a transition mechanism, giving a combination of encapsulation or translation, an IPv6-only underlay, and decapsulation or translation. For an IPv6-only network, connectivity to legacy IPv4 is either non-existent or provided by these mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6-only is not one thing but a family of statements about different parts of a network. An interface can be IPv6-only while the rest of the machine still speaks IPv4. A service can be IPv6-only if every header on the path is IPv6. An overlay can be IPv6-only if the tunnel inside is IPv6 even though the tunnel itself rides on IPv4. Naming the scope is the point, because each scope needs different work.

sections.title: The Global Picture
sections.content:
The RFC deals with four key questions: the status of IPv4 exhaustion, often considered one of the triggers to switch to IPv6; the number of IPv6 end users, a primary measure of adoption; the percentage of websites reachable over IPv6; and a report on public actions and policies. These parameters are monitored by the Regional Internet Registries and other institutions worldwide, as they provide a first-order indication of adoption.

On exhaustion, the RFC reports that there will be 29.3 billion networked devices by 2023, up from 18.4 billion in 2018, and asks whether the IPv4 address space can sustain that number. On one hand the registries report scarcity: the available pool of the five registries at the end of 2021 counted 5.2 million IPv4 addresses, while the reserved pool included another 12.1 million, for a total of 17.3 million, a fall of 5.5 percent year over year, and the total allocated pool equalled 3.685 billion addresses. On the other hand, address transfer and Network Address Translation counter exhaustion, with cloud service providers appearing to be the most active in buying IPv4 addresses, while NAT lets private addressing be used inside networks and limits the use of public addresses on the WAN-facing side. Architectural and operational issues remain, including multiple levels of translation such as Carrier-Grade NAT, which carry an economic and operational burden.

On users, the RFC aggregates the estimated number of IPv6-capable users against the total Internet users as of 1 January 2022: 1,207.61 million IPv6-capable users out of 4,093.69 million in total, a ratio of 29.5 percent, against 15.0 percent in January 2018. On web content, the share of websites accessible over IPv6 was 20.6 percent in January 2022, up from 11.4 percent in January 2018, and out of the world's top 500 sites, 203 were IPv6 enabled in January 2022. The RFC notes that not all websites are equal, since the largest content providers already support IPv6 and generate far more content than small websites.

On public actions, the RFC notes that higher adoption in certain countries has been achieved as a consequence of government action through regulation or incentive. It describes Belgium's 2012 agreement limiting the use of one IPv4 address per 16 customers behind NAT, whose economic burden on the ISPs induced a shift to IPv6; France's obligation that mobile carriers awarded 5G licences be IPv6 compatible; Germany's 2019 high-level road map for mandatory IPv6 in federal administration networks; the United States plan for 80 percent of federal IP-capable networks to be IPv6-only by 2025; and guidelines from China and India.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers say the change is real but incomplete. About three in ten Internet users can now reach the network over IPv6, and about a fifth of websites answer over it, but the biggest websites count for far more traffic than the smallest, so the content is more reachable than the headline website figure suggests. Government pressure has done a lot of the work in the countries that moved fastest.

sections.title: The Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes five scenarios. The sequence is not a road map: depending on their plans and requirements, service providers may adopt the scenarios in order or jump directly to a specific one.

Dual-Stack appears to be the most widely deployed IPv6 solution, about 50 percent. With it, IPv6 can be introduced together with other network upgrades, and many parts of network management and IT systems can still work in IPv4, which avoids a major upgrade of those systems, possibly the most difficult task in the transition. The cost and effort on the network management and IT systems upgrade are moderate, and the benefits are to start using IPv6 and save NAT costs. Its disadvantages in the long run are the duplication of network resources and states, and that it requires more IPv4 addresses, increasing both capital and operating expenses; even with private addresses behind Carrier-Grade NAT there is extra investment in the NAT devices, log storage and help desk. The RFC reports that of 346 operators participating in the World IPv6 Launch in June 2021, 108 exceed 50 percent of IPv6 traffic volume, 72 exceed 60 percent and 37 exceed 75 percent, and that the consensus to move to IPv6-only might be reasonable when IPv6 traffic volume is between 50 and 60 percent.

The IPv6-only overlay means the overlay tunnel between the endpoints of a network is based only on IPv6. Tunneling provides a way to use an existing IPv4 infrastructure to carry IPv6 traffic, so the approach helps maintain compatibility with the existing IPv4 base, but it is not a long-term solution, and IPv4 reachability must be provided for a long time to come over IPv6 for IPv6-only hosts.

The IPv6-only underlay uses IPv6 as the network protocol for all traffic delivery, with both the control and data planes based on IPv6. When operators transition to an IPv6 underlay, the ISP backbone should be IPv6-only, because Dual-Stack is not the best choice and the forwarding plane complexity on the Provider nodes should be kept simple as a backbone with a single protocol. IPv4 packets can still be tunnelled using a VPN over an IPv6-only backbone. The RFC notes that the current trend is to keep the IPv4 and MPLS data plane and run Dual-Stack to the edge nodes.

IPv4-as-a-Service ensures IPv4 support and can be a complex decision depending on economic aspects, policy and government regulation. It offers Dual-Stack service to users while letting the provider run IPv6-only in the network, typically the access network. Such transition technologies require far fewer IPv4 addresses, because they are more efficient and do not restrict the number of ports per subscriber, which reduces troubleshooting costs and removes operational issues related to permanent block listing of IPv4 address blocks. For deployments with many users or many hosts, even the full private address space is not enough, and Dual-Stack will likely lead to duplication of network resources and operations, which increases the amount of state information in the network.

IPv6-only is the final stage, when a complete network, end to end, no longer has IPv4, with no IPv4 address configured for network management or anything else. Since it means both underlay networks and overlay services are only IPv6, it will take longer to happen.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five ways to be partway there. Run both versions side by side, which is what most providers do, but it doubles the equipment and needs more IPv4 addresses. Carry IPv6 inside an IPv4 tunnel, which buys time but is not a destination. Run the network itself on IPv6 only, and tunnel the leftover IPv4 traffic over it. Offer IPv4 as a service on top of an IPv6-only network, which is what mobile operators do and which uses far fewer IPv4 addresses. Or drop IPv4 entirely, which is the end state and the slowest to reach.

sections.title: The Remaining Challenges
sections.content:
The RFC lists common challenges that were validated and discussed during several meetings and public events, noting that IPv6 has already been well proven in production but that some challenges remain, and that another ETSI document also discusses gaps that still exist in IPv6-related use cases.

On transition choices, the choice of method may depend on factors specific to the context, such as the IPv6 network design that fits the service requirements, the network operations and the deployment strategy. Fixed operators are mostly attached to a Dual-Stack architecture and many have already employed Carrier-Grade NAT, which boosts their ability to supply IPv4 connectivity for more years to come. Mobile operators face a different situation, since in some cases they are already stretching their IPv4 address space because translation limits have been reached; some choose Dual-Stack as an immediate mitigation, while others prefer IPv4-as-a-Service because Dual-Stack only mitigates and does not solve the scarcity issue completely. Enterprises are shielded from IPv4 depletion by their prevalent use of proxy and private addressing, so they lack the business requirement or technical justification to transition, and the ICT budget is often constrained; worldwide, and especially for small and medium-sized enterprises, adoption is late, because the engineers do not have much IPv6 experience and porting applications looks difficult.

On network management and operations, the RFC notes that some IPv6 products are not as field proven as IPv4 products even though conventional protocols already support IPv6, and that an incompatible vendor road map for new management features affects operator confidence. Deploying IPv6 requires policies and procedures to be adjusted and staff to be trained, and management applications and equipment may need to be reconfigured or replaced. Availability of both systems and training is necessary in areas such as addressing, where addresses can be assigned through Stateless Auto-Configuration or the stateful Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, with IP Address Management systems handling the technical differences and automating tasks such as address assignment or the management of DHCP services.

On performance, the RFC is careful. People tend to compare the performance of IPv6 against IPv4 to argue for or against the transition, and in some cases IPv6 behaving worse is used as an argument for avoiding full adoption. On packet loss and latency, measurement campaigns show that IPv4 is still performing better on failure rate, though the difference seems to have decreased, with reasons including endpoints with an unreachable IPv6 address, routing instability and firewall behaviour, while the worldwide average latency is slightly in favour of IPv6, and regions with an advanced deployment of IPv6 show better performance. The TCP connection time is still higher for IPv6, even if the gap has reduced. On customer experience it is not totally clear whether users perceive a better experience, though some content providers have publicly reported that users do, which could be explained by an IPv6 user connecting to an application hosted in an IPv6-only data centre without translations. The RFC's conclusion is that a definitive answer cannot be found on which version performs better: depending on the specific use case and application, IPv6 is better, and in others the same applies to IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: What is left is mostly about people and operations rather than the protocol. Enterprises have no business reason to move because private addresses hide the shortage from them, and they have no budget or experience. Operators need staff trained and management tools that are as proven as the ones they had for IPv4. On speed, the measurements do not settle the argument: IPv6 is slightly ahead on latency worldwide and clearly ahead in some countries, but IPv4 is still ahead on connection failures and connection setup times.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC groups the security concerns related to IPv6 into three classes: the basic IPv6 protocol, meaning the basic header, extension headers and addressing; IPv6-associated protocols, meaning ICMPv6, the Neighbor Discovery Protocol, Multicast Listener Discovery, DNS and DHCPv6; and Internet-wide IPv6 security, meaning filtering, denial of service and transition mechanisms. ICMPv6 performs error reporting and diagnostic functions. The Neighbor Discovery Protocol is a node discovery protocol that replaces and enhances the functions of ARP. Multicast Listener Discovery is used by IPv6 routers for discovering multicast listeners on a directly attached link, much as the Internet Group Management Protocol is used in IPv4.

These associated protocols are new compared to IPv4, so they add new security threats and the related solutions are still under discussion. Neighbor Discovery has known vulnerabilities: one document says to use IPsec, but that is impractical and not used, while SEcure Neighbor Discovery is not widely available, and applying host isolation may address many of the concerns.

On extension headers, they provide a hook for new features and are more flexible than IPv4 options, which adds complexity, since some security mechanisms may need to process the full chain of headers and some firewalls may filter on them; packets with extension headers may also be dropped on the public Internet. The original IPv6 Routing Header type 0 was deprecated because of possible remote traffic amplification. To mitigate attacks based on header chains and fragmentation, the initial header, the extension headers and the upper-layer header must all be in the first fragment, and the fragment header is forbidden in all Neighbor Discovery messages.

On privacy, IPv6 was designed to restore the end-to-end model with all nodes on networks using globally unique addresses, but that greater visibility on the Internet implies privacy concerns. IPv6 nodes can and typically do use privacy extensions to prevent tracking of their burned-in Media Access Control addresses, which are easily readable in the original modified 64-bit Extended Unique Identifier interface identifier format; stable IPv6 interface identifiers were also developed, and they affect privacy too. The RFC's own Security Considerations section says the document has no impact on the security properties of specific IPv6 protocols or transition tools.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 brought new protocols with it, notably the neighbour discovery that replaces ARP, and those have their own weaknesses that are still being worked on. Extension headers are flexible but give attackers more room, which is why the rules require the whole header chain to stay in the first fragment. Privacy cuts both ways too: unique addresses make tracking easier, and the privacy extensions that hide a device's hardware address have a stable counterpart that undoes it.

viz.caption: THE SCOPES OF THE TERM IPv6-ONLY

items.title: IPv6-only interface
items.text: The interface of a node is configured to forward only IPv6. A Dual-Stack interface is not an IPv6-only interface.

items.title: IPv6-only node
items.text: The node uses only IPv6, so all interfaces of the host have only IPv6 addresses.

items.title: IPv6-only service
items.text: Used if every packet header of the service session, from the host's interface to the content server's interface, is IPv6.

items.title: IPv6-only overlay
items.text: Used if all inner packet headers of the tunnels between their endpoints are IPv6.

items.title: IPv6-only underlay
items.text: Used if the data plane and control plane are IPv6, though not necessarily the management plane.

items.title: IPv6-only network
items.text: Used if every node in the network is IPv6-only. IPv4 should not exist in it.

items.title: IPv4-as-a-Service
items.text: IPv4 support given by a transition mechanism: encapsulation or translation, an IPv6-only underlay, then decapsulation or translation.

items.text: The method may depend on network design, operations and deployment strategy, and each operator needs its own evaluation.

items.title: Network management and operations

items.title: Performance
items.text: IPv6 is better in some use cases and IPv4 in others, so a definitive answer cannot be found.

items.title: Security and privacy
items.text: Autoconfiguration needs more attention, and the greater visibility of globally unique addresses raises privacy questions.
